newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's premier contains damaging party row.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's premier contains damaging party row.

text.p: Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres seemed on Thursday to have contained a damaging row within his ruling Socialist party over an accord with the conservative opposition on constitutional reforms.

The party's national committee, its top policy-making body, voted in the early hours of Thursday in favour of a deal struck with the opposition Social Democrats on changes to the country's political charter.

The changes would allow referendums in Portugal, open the door to electoral reform, with a possible reduction in the number of deputies, and give Portuguese emigrants the right to vote in presidential elections amongst other modifications.

Socialist members of parliament, where the government is four seats short of an absolute majority, had reacted angrily to the latter two proposals, rejecting them in a special meeting called on Tuesday night.

But the national committee, whose decisions are binding on party members, came down heavily in favour of the accord, voting by 41-2, with eight abstentions, at the late night meeting after Guterres told them that that the accord was the best deal the party could have achieved.
Reforms to the electoral system require a two-thirds parliamentary majority. The Socialists and the Social Democrats control between them 85 percent of the 230-seat parliament.
"Guterres blocks Socialist crisis," ran the headline in the Diario de Noticias newspaper on Thursday.
Constitutional reform was one of the election pledges made by the Socialists in their successful 1995 campaign which brought them back to power for the first time in a decade.
But Socialist parliamentarians said that they had not been sufficiently consulted during the negotiations with the conservative Social Democrats.
It was the second time in a week that Guterres had appeared set on a collision course with his parliamentary party.
The premier, a practising Roman Catholic, angered party members by announcing ahead of a vote last Thursday on liberalising Portugal's restrictive abortion laws that he personally opposed change.

His statement probably clinched the issue as a handful of Socialists joined the opposition to defeat the reform, proposed by the party's youth wing, and which had the backing of the Communists and their 15 votes.
Guterres was due to attend a special meeting of his parliamentary party on Thursday night to explain further the proposed constitutional changes and win over the doubters.
But party critics promised him a rough ride.
"On Tuesday, not one Socialist deputy voted in favour of this deal. The argument is going to continue," said veteran Socialist parliamentarian Manuel Alegre.
